OPEN
This is open, and cannot be resolved with a finite computation.
Let $n\geq 4$. Are there $n$ points in $\mathbb{R}^2$, no three on a line and no four on a circle, such that all pairwise distances are integers?
#213: [Er75f,p.106][Er83c][Er87b,p.172]
geometry | 
distances
Anning and Erdős [AnEr45] proved there cannot exist an infinite such set. Harborth constructed such a set when $n=5$. The best construction to date, due to Kreisel and Kurz [KK08], has $n=7$. 
Ascher, Braune, and Turchet [ABT20] have shown that there is a uniform upper bound on the size of such a set, conditional on the Bombieri-Lang conjecture. Greenfeld, Iliopoulou, and Peluse [GIP24] have shown (unconditionally) that any such set must be very sparse, in that if $S\subseteq [-N,N]^2$ has no three on a line and no four on a circle, and all pairwise distances integers, then\[\lvert S\rvert \ll (\log N)^{O(1)}.\]See also [130].

 Greenfeld, Iliopoulou, and Peluse state that any integer distance set in $[-N,N]^2$ must either be polylogarithmically small (as noted above), or have the vast majority of its points lying on a single line or circle. Presumably the searches for an $n=8$ polygon in general position with integer distances have not found a solution yet.
Allowing for a certain number of collinear triplets $(C)$ and/or concyclic quadruples $(Q)$, then minimizing C+Q was done with AI assistance for $n=8$. The 'best' solution it found for me thus far was a set of $4$ collinear points and $1$ concyclic quadruple, so that $C+Q=5$. Rather disappointingly, all points $P_1$ through $P_8$ were either on a line or a circle, thus being completely aligned with the conclusion from Greenfeld et al.. It appears that finding any 'relaxed' configuration albeit with some independent points not on a line or circle is nearly as difficult as the $n=8$ solution in general position.
In case anyone is interested, the (somewhat trivial) solution found was $P_1 = (0, 528)$, $P_2 = (0, -528)$, $P_3 = (-630, 312)$, $P_4 = (-630, -312)$, $P_5 = (-896, 0)$, $P_6 = (-605, 0)$, $P_6 = ( -171, 0)$ and $P_8 = (704, 0)$. Primitive polygon diameter is $D=1600$ and characteristic $s =1$ (Recall the $n=7$ solution by Kreisel-Kurz had $s=2002$). If someone could find a lower $C+Q$ they are welcome to try!
